headline: Found 107-111 Central Street preferably preserved; motions to preserve 399 Lexington Street additions failed; approved $1200 for Stonehurst landscaping.
summary: The meeting covered demolition delay hearings for 399 Lexington Street, 103-105 Central Street, and 107-111 Central Street, plus development reviews for 51 Bacon Street and 962 Main Street. Members found 107-111 Central Street preferably preserved and 103-105 Central Street not preferably preserved, and did not find the 399 Lexington Street additions preferably preserved. They also approved a $1200 request for fall landscaping at Stonehurst and a letter of support for 20 Felton Street.
decisions: Did not find the east woodshed addition at 399 Lexington Street preferably preserved; motion failed 2-4.
Did not find the west wing addition at 399 Lexington Street preferably preserved; motion failed 1-5.
Found the house at 103-105 Central Street not preferably preserved, 6-0.
Found 51 Bacon Street not historically significant, 6-0.
Found the gas station at 962 Main Street not historically significant, 6-0.
Approved the $1200 request for fall landscaping at Stonehurst, 6-0.
Found the building at 20 Felton Street historically significant and approved writing a letter of support for replacing the siding and windows, 6-0.
Postponed officer elections because a commissioner was absent.

Chair: Reading and Description of Correspondence: 
The Building Department notified the Commission of an emergency demolition at 59 Farnum 
Road. The house was condemned. Commissioner Isaacson said the house did not appear to 
be historically significant. 
The Law Department responded to the Commission’s request for information on what 
happens when the Building Department doesn’t forward a demolition application within the 
time outlined in the ordinance. They said that the Historical Commission should proceed as 
usual and follow their timeline when they do receive the applications. The procedure should 
not change.  
Jordan Tannenbaum, former member of the Historical Commission, joined the meeting to 
give an update on the proposed changes to the Section 106 review process at the national 
level. He said that the proposed changes would eliminate review by consulting parties, such 
as historical commissions and the public. He requested that the public and the Waltham 
Historical Commission join other organizations in sending their objections and comments 
when the public comment period opens. 
    
5.   Chair: Public Hearings: 
Demolition Delay Hearings: 
399 Lexington Street (Farmhouse additions at Chapel Hill Chancy Hall School) 
Gwen Pojasek, CFO, represented the property. She shared photos of the building and 
explained that they planned to demolish only the one-story east and west additions to the 
farmhouse because of their poor condition. They planned to renovate and restore the core of 
the house. Commissioner Daly shared her report on the history of the building. It was built by 
Jonas Clark Sr. in 1825. These additions appear on the 1854 map. The surrounding area has 
extensive and significant history. The Clark family and descendants remained in the house 
until the 1980s when the school acquired the house. Commissioner Isaacson recommended 
that the school explore options for preserving the additions. Commissioner Daly agreed. 
Commissioner Egirous noted the considerable decay visible in the photos of the wings and 
there was discussion of the condition of the house.  
Commissioner Daly moved to find the east woodshed addition preferably preserved.

The Historical Commission offered to assist the school with creating historic signage for the

103-105 Central Street 
Ron Cincotta represented the property. He said they wanted to demolish the house and 
replace it with two new townhouses. Commissioner Daly shared her history report. The 
house was built in 1898 and owned by Robert Treat Paine, although he never lived there. It 
was most likely built as housing for workers in the area. Although the house was built by 
Robert Treat Paine and listed in the MACRIS database, no one of historic significance lived 
in the house. There was discussion of the plans for a replacement building.  
Commissioner Daly moved to find the house not preferably preserved.

107-111 Central Street 
Ron Cincotta also represented this property. He planned to demolish the house and replace it 
with two townhouses, similar to the neighboring property. Commissioner Daly shared her 
history report. “The house at 107-111 Central Street was built in 1834 for its first owner, Mrs. 
Lucy Sawtelle. The house forms an integral part of the built environment surrounding the 
Francis Cabot Lowell mill, founded in 1814 and owned by the Boston Manufacturing 
Company. It is one of the earliest houses built on Central Street. Since 1834, the building was 
the home of two families for almost 140 years: the Sawtelle family and the Olivo-Piantedosi 
family.” There are very few houses left in that area from that period. 
Commissioner Daly moved to find 107-111 Central Street preferably preserved. 
Commissioner Dufromont seconded.

There was discussion of the report submitted. The report says the renovation and restoration 
project was complete, and a final walkthrough took place. Commissioner Isaacson said that 
the Historical Commission was supposed to have a final walkthrough. He requested that 
Commissioner Wilson ask the CPC about it. Commissioner Russo also asked that the reports 
from the Stonehurst curator have more details. Commissioner Dufromont agreed. 
Commissioner Isaacson said he would have to ask Bob Waters, the planning director.  
8.  Wellington House: Monthly Report & Update:  
     
Commissioner Isaacson drove by the house and there had been no more progress on the      
exterior.  
9.   Liaison & Subcommittee Reports:  
Fernald: The Chapel was going to be demolished. It was built in 1960 so it would not come 
before the Historical Commission. 
Community Preservation Committee (CPC): Chloe-Rose Crouch represented 20 Felton 
Street, the Community Day Center, for a letter of support for their application. The 
application was for restoration of the historic building. It was built in 1890 and was originally 
used as a storage facility for meat delivered from the Swift Company of Chicago by train. 
Commissioner Isaacson said they don’t know for sure what the building looked like 
originally. The earliest images available show a similar looking structure, although there have 
been renovations over the years. The MACRIS form and more current photos of the building 
were shared. Commissioners were concerned about the fourth side of the building that 
seemed inaccessible due to its proximity to the building next door. Ms. Crouch said they 
were not planning to replace the siding on that fourth side. Commissioners requested that 
they investigate having that siding replaced to prevent further rotting and to preserve the 
whole building. There was discussion of what materials would be appropriate for the 
renovation, wood or more modern materials for preservation.  
Commissioner Daly moved to find the building historically significant, to write a letter 
of support for the application to replace the siding and windows, and that the 
Commission looks forward to working with the Community Day Center on materials.  
Commissioner Russo seconded.
